facts.claim: We have visually observed less than 0.001% of the deep seafloor, which is an area approximately a tenth of the size of Belgium.
facts.quote: we have visually observed less than 0.001%, a total area approximately a tenth of the size of Belgium.

facts.claim: Sixty-five percent of all in situ visual seafloor observations in the dataset were within 200 nm of only three countries: the United States, Japan, and New Zealand.
facts.quote: Sixty-five percent of all in situ visual seafloor observations in our dataset were within 200 nm of only three countries: the United States, Japan, and New Zealand.

facts.claim: Ninety-seven percent of all dives compiled have been conducted by just five countries: the United States, Japan, New Zealand, France, and Germany.
facts.quote: Ninety-seven percent of all dives we compiled have been conducted by just five countries: the United States, Japan, New Zealand, France, and Germany.

facts.claim: With the current average rate of new map generation of ∼3.2% of total seafloor area annually, the global seafloor could be mapped in approximately 20 years.
facts.quote: With the current average rate of new map generation of ∼3.2% of total seafloor area annually, we predict that the global seafloor could be mapped in approximately 20 years.

facts.claim: Over 14% of the ocean fell under the category of globally important marine areas and most of this area (88%) is not yet protected.
facts.quote: Over 14% of the ocean fell under this category and most of this area (88%) is not yet protected.

research.angle: Humanity has visually observed a minuscule and geographically biased fraction of the deep seafloor, with the vast majority of mapping efforts concentrated near only five countries.
research.verdict: The evidence confirms that direct visual observation of the deep seafloor is extremely limited and heavily skewed toward specific nations.
research.caveat: The data highlights a significant geographical bias in observation rather than a total lack of mapping effort in all regions.
